body_markdown:
*Welcome back to[Reputation Management](https://www.hagerty.com/media/category/advice/reputation-management/) ! We are again revealing the underbelly of local automotive retailers—places like car dealers and service shops—with fictional service tales inspired by real customer reviews. How do we make these stories seem like they could really happen? Because of my years of experience with a Fortune 500 automotive retailer as a—you guessed it—reputation manager.* *—Sajeev*


Back in the 2010s, getting people to use social media wasn’t difficult. Everyone wanted to explore these virtual communities and share stories or new ideas, and they would recommend these tech platforms to their friends. I was lucky in my role as a Social Media/Reputation Manager for CarCountry to be in the thick of it, not only because of how early I joined the industry (May 2010), but because I applied this new technology to the staid and guarded world of automotive retail.


Part of running social media for car dealerships involved promoting the vehicles on your lot. It used to be as simple as making a post on your “Facebook Business” page, watching your post generate comments, and collecting the resulting phone calls/emails. The business page was a lead generator just like Cars.com, Edmunds, or Car Gurus, except it never took a cut of the deal. While posting up a 2011 Mercury Milan was akin to farting in a crowded elevator, the all-new 2011 Ford Explorer was bound to get a like, comment, and an off-line phone call.


The Great Recession was well in the rearview mirror, and America was ready to party in more approachable crossover utilities and virtual plazas accessed by computers and those newfangled smartphones. Facebook and the front-wheel drive Explorer were made for each other. But don’t take my word for it: Ford[even unveiled the CUV](https://mashable.com/archive/ford-explorer-web-reveal) on its Facebook page.


Does this make you want to join Facebook in 2010?


Facebook | Ford


The Blue Oval gang was ahead of its time, even rolling out a teaser image of its new grille before the reveal, as if in celebration of its Facebook page breaking 30,000 fans. Pay no attention to the future Facebook scandals and the horrors of MyFordTouch cabin electronics, because we were *livin’ it up* on social media back in July 2010.


Facebook | Ford


*******


Rocky Wahl was the general manager (GM) of one of the largest Ford dealerships in the Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) area. He was young enough to embrace social media platforms, and old enough to know not to fight the newly minted social media manager (yours truly) hired by his CarCountry overlords.


Wahl was one of the easy conquests (as it were), because other CarCountry GMs were very precious with their Facebook Business pages. Some folks wouldn’t cede ownership even after I made it clear to them that they still had full access to their page, and that I would also help with regular upkeep (and a future need for reputation management). With hardheaded individuals, I’ve been known to threaten fire and brimstone from the VP of Legal if they wouldn’t relinquish control of their dealership’s branded Facebook pages.


That wasn’t bluster, either. Like it or not, every Facebook page for CarCountry came under my umbrella, but folks like Rocky embraced the extra help. After acquiring a Samsung Galaxy S (with a 5-megapixel camera!) for Christmas in 2010, he’d photograph fun cars on the lot to post on Facebook. The dude was marketing-savvy, wisely avoiding V-6 Mustangs or any Ford Fusion. So when it came time to follow in Ford’s footsteps, he unveiled his first 2011 Explorer on our Facebook page.


How I long for the days when Facebook posts were written by normal human beings.


Facebook


I loved Rocky’s content, grammar quirks aside. He knew to keep his personal feelings on his personal Facebook page, and he engaged the customer with skill both in person and on the dealership’s Facebook. Or so I thought. Shortly after the post you see above went live, a customer “posted” to our corporate page with a comment that strikes fear in a Reputation Manager’s heart, no matter the year in which it was posted:


> “Tsk tsk, I see my post was deleted from the 15th, because I checked out a new Explorer and you were rude to me. I will never come back and I’ll tell everyone to do the same thing. Lost a customer forever!”


I immediately emailed Rocky, informing him that deleting people’s posts is generally a horrible idea for any local business. That’s rich coming from my ivory tower, but I know the landscape and how people perceive this business. “I didn’t do that,” was his response. I bristled, but I know GMs are quickly scanning emails on their smartphones, hoping that possible confrontations from a corporate stooge like myself would disappear with a terse reply.


After informing Rocky that only two people have access to the Facebook page and one of us isn’t stupid enough to delete a post (I said it nicer than that), I told him to stop letting others use his Facebook credentials at work and consider my proposal for a response. I rang him up on said Samsung Galaxy S, because said idea required an explanation:


*“Rocky, you know the story of the salesman who ate an $800 hamburger over lunch?”*


*“Dude, everyone in the car business knows that. And yes, I see where this is going.”*


We like to have fun in the car business, and stories like the $800 hamburger are a fantastic coping mechanism for the job you willingly signed up for. If you work in the car business and take a lunch, you’re bound to lose a big sale because that’s when walk-in customers are shopping. That burger better be delicious, because you also lost about $800 in commissions while you were eating it.


I’m going easy on Rocky, because he’s one of the “good ones” who will embrace new technology, adapting to whatever comes his way. He even researched the customer’s name via his ADP dealer terminal while we were talking. Apparently she was looking at an older Explorer on the used car lot before she went inside to gawk at the new one.


“We need to apologize in our (public) reply, and offer $500 off the used Explorer she was looking at,” I said.


Shockingly, he didn’t balk. I didn’t know what number to use, but $500 sounded big enough to ensure he would never delete a post again. And if I felt that way, odds were that the general public in DFW would feel the same. So I whipped up a response, emailed it back to Rocky, and held my breath:


> “Hello (NAME), thank you for bringing this to my attention. It is our policy to not delete anyone’s Facebook post and I will be reminding to our team of this tomorrow morning. In the meantime, if you can please call me to make up for this, I would like to offer you $500 off that Explorer you were looking at. My name is Rocky, my number is (REDACTED), and I look forward to hearing from you.”


Again, he didn’t balk. In less than an hour, she replied to us with positivity and a promise to call Rocky back. Crisis averted: This mere social media manager had officially earned his Reputation Management cape. I got an email two days later from Rocky, saying that a 2009 Explorer was sold with my help and we now have a customer for life.


Like any pro in the car business, Rocky knows how to hit a home run when his staff offers him the right pitch. And CarCountry’s social media manager pitches the slowest of slow meatballs. Toss that ball at the right speed, and job security in a huge corporation is guaranteed. The recession is over, and someone just created a new form of public relations … on Facebook, of all places.


*The Reputation Manager will return…*
